While looking for a complete collaborative filtering/recommender systems library in R, the only one I came across is "recommenderlab" (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/recommenderlab/index.html) which is more directed towards faster prototyping for new recommender system algorithms in academia. My proposal is a fast, complete and generic recommender systems library in R targeted towards professional developers. Would there be much value to this? If so, I'd like to get in touch with interested mentors for the project.

Thanks,
Abhinav

messages.subject: Idea Proposal : Non-convex optimization.
messages.subject_clean: Idea Proposal : Non-convex optimization.
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

The proposal is to implement algorithms for  wide avariety of non-convex optimization problems. I looked for R pacakges which solve problems I prose to implement, but I could not find a coherent one encompassing a lot of such problems. Broadly, I am keen to solve problems in which non-convexity aries via known structures like low rank and/or sparsity, for which we have algorithms with theoretical guarantees.
I would start with compressive sensing/sparse recovery and implement convex relaxation methods as well as Alternating Minimization style algorithms like Iterative Hard Thresholding (IHT), GradeS etc. After that, I will move forward with algorthms for matrix low rank regression, robust PCA, matrix completion, dictionary learning, phase retrieval etc

Please let me know if this is a feasible project, and if anybody is interested in mentoring me.

Thanks and regards,
Enayat
ena...@iitk.ac.in

messages.subject_clean: Update for R GSoC Mentors and Students
messages.body_plain:
We have approximately one week before student applications open.

This email contains some notes for both prospective project mentors and
prospective students.

Students:

If you have identified a project you want to work on, you should be
communicating with the mentors.  Please accomplish any test tasks,
figure out how to compile required packages, get your build environment
in place, and start working on your application.  Student applications
for successful projects tend to run to about 10 pages or more if
printed, so don't delay on working on your application!

Mentors:

Please review your project idea pages on the wiki:
https://github.com/rstats-gsoc/gsoc2017/wiki/

Make sure that your idea page identifies:
- mentor names and email addresses
- tests for the student
- descriptions of skills required
- milestones for the first, second, and third month of the project
  (** this is a new Google request, just passed along recently! **)

Toby and I will be inviting mentors this week.  If we don't know you
and your contact information is not on your idea pages, you won't get
an invitation, and won't get a project. If your contact information
isn't on your idea page, you aren't likely to get good student
interest.

If your project doesn't have an idea page, even if you've identified a
desired student for your proposed project already, you won't get a
slot.  Google requires these project idea pages, and we use them in our
org application and as an organizational aid at the beginning of GSoC!.

The next few weeks will be quite busy for all of us, so your active
participation and patience are both appreciated.

Regards,

Brian

--
Brian G. Peterson
http://braverock.com/brian/
Ph: 773-459-4973
IM: bgpbraverock

messages.subject: Re: Sentometrics
messages.subject_clean: Sentometrics
messages.body_plain:
Hi Gustavo,

Sentiment analysis is not easy. The same word or phrase can have vastly different sentiment depending on its context and factors about its situation which may not be evident from the text. The idea of plotting sentiment as a function of time requires a detailed history of each term with dates, and that is in no way easy, because there are tens of thousands if not hundreds of thousands of such terms you might want to cover.

Would your proposal be better suited to improving R's existing sentiment analysis, whether in the tm package or elsewhere? Seth Grimes is holding this symposium and may be able to suggest possible co-mentors if your revised proposal meets with approval of the mentors:

http://2017.sentimentsymposium.com/

Who knows, maybe Seth wants to co-mentor. He's certainly well-connected. The only way to find out is to ask him so I've cc'ed him. I would be happy to co-mentor if an already-invited mentor would like to mentor. I have plenty of NLP experience, but the other R mentors are skeptical of my appreciation of adjusting symbolic regression for actual model degrees of freedom and my distaste for the size of the finance sector, so who knows whether they will let me this year.

If you want an easy task, how about using the new Google Trends API as a complement to sentiment analysis in the tm package? Here is a JavaScript snippet which uses the new Google Trends API to get the past week of information about the Making Work Pay tax credit:

https://runkit.com/58cc73351463760015f5f3a5/58cc73351463760015f5f3a6

That would be great to have in R's tm package, and it's easy but you would still need multiple passes for comparable outputs, because Google does some kind of de-normalization leaving the y-axis indeterminate, but scaled around the range 0-100. Why they don't use logarithms instead is beyond me.

Best regards,
Jim

messages.subject_clean: Update for R GSoC Mentors and Students
messages.body_plain:
Student applications open tomorrow (Monday, 20 March).

Students should follow the application template:
https://github.com/rstats-gsoc/gsoc2017/wiki/application-template
and post links to your applications on the summerofcode.withgoogle.com <http://summerofcode.withgoogle.com> site.

Applications should be created as Google Docs with comments turned on
for anyone with the link.  Expect comments from your mentors, and other
R mentors.  You can revise the application to finish off incomplete bits
or based on the comments you receive until you do a final submit, at
which point your application is not editable.

I have invited all 65 mentors listed on the project idea pages for which
I had contact information. If you received an invitastion, you should
accept it and complete the mentor registration process for GSoC 2017.
Where mentor email addresses were not listed on the idea page, I
followed links to get to an email address.  If you didn't get a mentor
invitation from Google to the summerofcode site, that implies that you
are not listed as a mentor for a project proposal, or did not put
contact information there.  Please correct your oversight and email Toby
and me, and we'll work it out.

As in prior years, mentors should read and comment on all draft student
applications that are in your areas of expertise, not just applications
for your favored project(s).  Toby and I will be relying on the overall
quality of the application and feedback from mentors to make our slot
requests to Google.  Last year Google removed the 'official' ranking
mechanism, so feedback from mentors is even more important.

Please make public comments on the draft applications with constructive
feedback for the student applicants.  Please communicate in private
about any serious issues, relative ranking of multiple applications for
the same project, or anything that you're not certain should be seen by
the student.

We are prohibited by Google from telling any student applicant they have
been accepted or rejected, and we won't know for weeks anyway, once
slots are final.  Google reserves the announcement of student acceptance
for themselves.

Google's deadlines are firm, there will be no exceptions or extensions.
Make sure you get everything done by the times listed in the official
timeline.

Thank you and good luck,

Brian

messages.subject_clean: Just in time: seeking mentors for hastening phylogenetics algotithms with CUDA
messages.body_plain:
Hello there!

I'm a Computer Science masters degree studant that use to research massively parallel algorithms at the HPC research group of my university (more information here <http://dgp.cnpq.br/dgp/espelhogrupo/7985061476854055>). The subject of my undergraduate term paper was "CUDA programming for Comparative Phylogenetics", wich in turn yelds the development of a parallel version of the software SUNPLIN. The original version of SUNPLIN <https://bmcbioinformatics.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/1471-2105-14-324> is known as the fastest sequential algorithm for computation of patristic distances, a very time-consuming operation. In other hand, the parallel version of it is able to speedup the execution by up to 74 times in comparsion to the sequencial version, acording to the first benchmarks.

The parallel version of SUNPLIN is a C++/CUDA standalone application, for performance purposes. This fact can prevent the use of most users wich are mainly R users and therefore accustomed to its facilities. My aim is to build a convenient R package that wraps SUNPLIN calls to GPU, is CRAN compliant and is easily installable and manageable.

Hope there's some Interested ones out there!

Is a pleasure to meet you guys,

Evandro Carrijo Taquary
Federal University of Goiás

messages.body_plain:
---------- Forwarded message ----------
From: Google Summer of Code <summerofco...@google.com>
Date: Fri, Mar 31, 2017 at 11:35 AM
Subject: GSoC 2017: Final PDF review and Slot Allocation
To: bgpbra...@gmail.com

Hi Brian Peterson,

The student submission period is nearly over - you can expect a lot of proposals coming in over these last 72 hours! We know you are all quite busy responding to students and giving them feedback on their draft proposals. In the next phase of GSoC, you select which of these proposals you choose for GSoC projects.
Reviewing Final PDF Proposals: April 3 - 16

The deadline for students to submit their Final PDF proposal is Monday, April 3rd at 16:00 UTC.
Students without Final PDF proposals cannot be accepted, and there will be no exceptions.

After 16:00 UTC April 3rd, org members will be able to see the Final PDFs submitted by students.

April 3rd 16:00 UTC is also the deadline for students to submit a proof of enrollment in an eligible university program. Students who fail to do this are ineligible for GSoC this year. We will be reviewing the forms and students will have a chance to resubmit if there are any problems.

Your decision about whether or not to select a student should be based on the Final PDF proposal. You will also be able to reference the draft proposal -- but should not make your decision based on it. A draft proposal is intended to be used to view the comment thread and maybe see how the student interacted with you and responded to comments, etc. Do not use it to let the student make more changes after the deadline. That is not fair to all the other applicants.
Want to Mentor?

If you are interested in being a mentor for a given proposal then you can click the purple “Want to Mentor” button to help your Org Admin know that you are interested. This is particularly helpful for the org admins when determining if they have enough mentors for their slot requests.
Slots Request - deadline April 17 16:00 UTC

Org Admins will request a minimum and maximum number of project slots. Slots should only be requested for projects where there is at least one confirmed mentor and where the student has a good chance of succeeding. Do not accept "okay" proposals. New orgs will likely only receive 1-2 slots, no matter how many they request.

April 17th is also the deadline for students to have any re-submitted proof of enrollment forms approved. Note that students with invalid forms will not appear in your list of student projects you can choose from starting April 19th (when slots are announced).

All Org Admins should read Slot Allocation and Project Selection <https://developers.google.com/open-source/gsoc/help/slot-allocation> for more detailed information.
Upcoming Important Dates

April 3 16:00 UTC: Mentors and Org Admins review student draft proposals and give students feedback on their proposals.
April 3 - 16: Review all submitted student proposals with your org and consider how many you want to select and how many you can handle. Decide on the minimum/maximum number of student slots to request.
April 17, 16:00 UTC: Deadline to submit slot requests (OAs enter requests)
April 19, 16:00 UTC: Slot allocations are announced by Google
April 19 - 24 16:00 UTC : Select the proposals to become student projects. At least 1 mentor must be assigned to each project before it can be selected. (OAs enter selections)
April 24 - May 4: Google Program Admins will do another review of student eligibility
May 4: Accepted GSoC students/projects are announced
May 4 - 29: Community Bonding Period
May 30: Coding begins!
June 26-30: First evaluation period - mentors evaluate students, students evaluate mentors

If you haven’t done so already, be sure to read the Roles and Responsibilities <https://developers.google.com/open-source/gsoc/help/responsibilities> to understand what is expected of you and of students during the program.

Please contact us at gsoc-s...@google.com with any questions.

Google Open Source Programs Office

This email was sent to bgpbra...@gmail.com <http://bgp...@gmail.com>.

You are receiving this email because of your participation in Google Summer of Code 2017.
https://summerofcode.withgoogle.com

To leave the program and stop receiving all emails, you can go to your profile <https://summerofcode.withgoogle.com/dashboard/profile/> and request deletion of your program profile.

For any questions, please contact gsoc-s...@google.com. Replies to this message go to an unmonitored mailbox.

messages.subject: [GSoC-R] Schedules, Deliverables, Next Steps
messages.subject_clean: [GSoC-R] Schedules, Deliverables, Next Steps
messages.body_plain:
Student applications for GSoC 2017 close on Monday, April 3rd at 16:00
UTC.

Google's deadlines are firm, and there are no exceptions, for any
reason.

Students:
You should be communicating as much as possible with the mentors for
your desired project and revising your applications.  Waiting till the
last minute is not usually a sign of a project likely to succeed.
Please try to finalize your application and upload the final PDF well
in advance of the deadline, after addressing any questions or comments
from your mentors or any other R project mentor.  Applications are
fixed after the final PDF is uploaded.

Mentors:
Some mentors have not accepted their invitations.  If you're having
trouble, please contact Toby or me immediately, and we'll try to help
you.

Right Now: You should be communicating with your applicants about their
applications.  Please raise any and all concerns that you have about
the application using comments in the Google doc, per Google
guidelines.  Give your students as much feedback as you can on the
application, while they still have time to make it better.

After April 3rd, Toby and I will be doing a first review of submitted
applications.  We will be contacting mentors individually for feedback
where necessary.  After April 3rd, we also need you to do a few things
on the Google Summer of Code system:

1> We need you to select 'Want to Mentor' on an application for a
project where you are listed as a mentor, or on the strongest
application for the project where there are multiple applications for a
single project.

2> We also need you to comment on all applications for projects where
you are listed as a mentor in the 'Comment on this Proposal' section at
the bottom of the proposal page.  Please provide a succinct summary of
your feelings on the application.  These comments are visible to other
R mentors only, not to the students.  We want all mentors to comment on
all proposals for a project you are a listed mentor for.

3> We *want*, but cannot require, that you comment on other student
applications for proposed projects that you will not be mentoring this
summer.  If you have time to comment on draft applications this weekend
in your area of expertise, please do so to help out the students in
thinking about their projects.  In any case, please comment on projects
next week where you have some expertise.  Google used to require all
mentors to vote on applications, but that was removed from the process
last year.  Your input is still very valuable to Toby and me as we
review applications and make slot requests.

Slot request to Google will happen no later than April 17th, per the
Google Deadline.  April 19th-24th Toby and I will communicate with
mentors and allocate the slots we've received from Google.

On May 4th, accepted projects will be announced by Google.

Between April 3rd and May 4th, Google prohibits mentors and
organizations from telling students whether or not their proposal has
been accepted.  Students, please don't ask.  Mentors, please don't
tell.  Google takes a very dim view of breaking this rule.

Regards,

Brian

--
Brian G. Peterson
